intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that brachyolmia type 4 with mild epiphyseal and metaphyseal changes (BCYM4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PAPSS2 gene (also called ATPSK2) on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Brachyolmia type 4 with mild epiphyseal and metaphyseal changes is an autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia that mainly affects the spine. Patients have short-trunk short stature, normal intelligence, rectangular or flattened vertebral bodies with irregular endplates and narrow intervertebral discs, and variable epiphyseal and metaphyseal changes of the tubular bones (Ahmad et al., 1998; Miyake et al., 2012). Miyake et al. (2012) stated that PAPSS2 mutations give rise to a range of phenotypes from brachyolmia to spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia.

checks.explanation: AR form and spine involvement stated.

paragraphs.text: Ahmad et al. (1998) described an inbred kindred spanning 8 generations from a remote area of Pakistan with a distinct form of spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (SEMD). They evaluated 16 affected individuals, 11 males and 5 females. Clinical findings were short stature evident at birth, short bowed lower limbs, mild brachydactyly, kyphoscoliosis, abnormal gait, enlarged knee joints, precocious osteoarthropathy, and normal intelligence. On radiographs there was delayed epiphyseal ossification at the hips and knees, platyspondyly with irregular end plates, narrowed joint spaces, and diffuse early osteoarthritic changes, mostly in the spine and hands. Mild metaphyseal abnormalities were seen, predominantly at the hips and knees. Ahmad et al. (1998) considered this phenotype distinct from other autosomal recessive forms of SEMD because of the mild metaphyseal involvement, the type of brachydactyly, and the absence of loose joints or other clinical findings.

paragraphs.text: Miyake et al. (2012) studied 3 affected members of a Turkish family with autosomal recessive brachyolmia, as well as 3 more patients with a similar phenotype (2 Japanese and 1 Korean). All 6 had short-trunk short stature that became noticeable during childhood, with normal intelligence and facies. Radiographic features included rectangular vertebral bodies with irregular endplates and narrow intervertebral discs, precocious calcification of the rib cartilages, short femoral necks, and mildly shortened metacarpals. The spinal changes were very similar in all 6 patients, but epiphyseal and metaphyseal changes of the tubular bones varied.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with compound heterozygous PAPSS2 mutations, Noordam et al. (2009) found very low DHEAS levels and increased androgen levels. They explained that the DHEA sulfotransferase SULT2A1 converts DHEA to its inactive sulfate ester, DHEAS, which prevents DHEA from being converted to an active androgen, and that SULT2A1 needs 3-prime-phosphoadenosine-5-prime-phosphosulfate (PAPS) for its catalytic activity.

paragraphs.text: Ahmad et al. (1998) concluded from the pedigree of a large inbred Pakistani kindred that this form of SEMD has autosomal recessive inheritance. Consanguineous loops could explain why all affected individuals were homozygous for the abnormal allele. Miyake et al. (2012) also found autosomal recessive inheritance in a Turkish family with brachyolmia.

paragraphs.text: Noordam et al. (2009) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the PAPSS2 gene in a girl with premature pubarche and androgen excess. When human SULT2A1 was coincubated in vitro with wildtype or mutant PAPSS2 proteins, the mutations were shown to be inactivating. Noordam et al. (2009) concluded that PAPSS2 deficiency is a monogenic adrenocortical cause of androgen excess.

paragraphs.text: Using exon capture and next-generation sequencing in 3 affected members of a Turkish family with autosomal recessive brachyolmia, Miyake et al. (2012) identified a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the PAPSS2 gene (c.337_338insG; p.A113GfsX18). In 3 further patients with similar brachyolmia phenotypes (2 Japanese and 1 Korean), they found loss-of-function mutations in PAPSS2. One patient was homozygous for IVS3+2delT. The other 2 were compound heterozygous, one for c.616-634del19 (p.V206SfsX9) and c.1309-1310delAG (p.R437GfsX19), and the other for c.480_481insCGTA (p.K161RfsX6) and c.661delA (p.I221SfsX40).

agent.process_note: I read all 4 papers in full. All of them were available only as abstracts. The papers name the causal gene PAPSS2 (called ATPSK2 by Faiyaz ul Haque et al., 1998) and map it to 10q23-q24. No reference data were supplied, so I left out the gene's MIM number. Faiyaz ul Haque et al. (1998) reported a nonsense mutation, but the abstract does not give it. The Noordam et al. (2009) abstract does not specify the compound heterozygous mutations or mention any skeletal findings. So neither paper has an allelic variant entry of its own. Miyake et al. (2012) does not say which Japanese or Korean patient carried which variants, so I left that unstated.
